body_html:
A generative engine optimization strategy is a step-by-step plan for getting your content found, understood and cited by AI search tools such as Google's AI Overviews, AI Mode and ChatGPT search. It starts with crawler access, then answer-first content, clear structure, real expertise, off-site reputation and a way to measure citations.

GEO in brief

Generative engine optimization (GEO) is the work of becoming a source that AI search tools quote, mention or link when they write an answer. The term comes from a research paper, "GEO: Generative Engine Optimization" by Aggarwal and colleagues, accepted at the KDD 2024 conference. For the full definition and how it relates to labels like AEO and AI SEO, read what generative engine optimization is and how it works; this guide focuses on the steps.

How GEO differs from SEO

Less than the hype suggests. Google's own guidance on AI features and your website says there are no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, and no special optimizations necessary. A page needs to be indexed and eligible to show in Search with a snippet. The same SEO fundamentals apply.

What changes is the unit of success. Classic SEO aims for a ranking and a click. GEO aims for inclusion in an answer, which might be a citation, a mention of your brand, or a link the reader may or may not click. That shifts some priorities:

  • Passages matter more than pages. AI tools often lift a few sentences, so each section should make sense on its own.
  • Clarity beats cleverness. A plain, direct answer is easier to quote than a clever intro.
  • Your reputation off-site counts. AI answers draw on reviews, directories, forums and other sites, not just your own pages.
  • More than one engine. Google, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Copilot and others each have their own crawlers and sources.

How AI search engines choose sources

None of these companies publishes a full formula, so be skeptical of anyone who claims to know one. What is documented is useful, though.

Google says AI Overviews and AI Mode may use a "query fan-out" technique: running several related searches on subtopics to gather supporting pages. That means a page can be cited for a sub-question even if it doesn't rank for the main query. Covering the natural follow-up questions on a topic gives you more chances to be picked.

Other engines rely on their own crawlers. OpenAI's crawler documentation explains that OAI-SearchBot is used to surface websites in ChatGPT search, and recommends allowing it in robots.txt if you want to appear there. It's separate from GPTBot, which collects content that may be used for model training. You can allow one and block the other.

A generative engine optimization strategy in 7 steps

Here's the practical work, roughly in the order I'd tackle it.

1. Make sure AI crawlers can reach you

  • Check robots.txt, your CDN and any firewall or bot-protection settings. Security tools sometimes block crawlers you want.
  • Decide on each bot deliberately: Googlebot for Search (including AI features), OAI-SearchBot for ChatGPT search, and training crawlers like GPTBot or Google-Extended based on your own policy.
  • Confirm key pages are indexed in Google Search Console and aren't blocked by noindex or nosnippet by mistake.

2. Put the answer first

  • Open each page or section with a direct, one- to three-sentence answer to the question it targets.
  • Follow with detail, examples and context. Think of the first paragraph as the part most likely to be quoted.
  • Use question-style headings that match how people actually ask.

3. Structure content so passages stand alone

  • Use descriptive H2 and H3 headings, short paragraphs, and real lists for steps or criteria.
  • Avoid sections that only make sense if you read the one before ("as mentioned above").
  • Keep important information in text, not only in images, PDFs or interactive widgets. Google's guidance specifically calls out keeping important content available in textual form.

This is the focus of my content structure work for AI search.

4. Show real expertise

  • Name the author and explain their experience.
  • Add first-hand detail: your process, real examples, what you've seen work and not work.
  • Cite primary sources when you state facts, and keep numbers current.

5. Use structured data that matches the page

Google is clear that no special schema is required for AI features. But structured data still helps search engines understand who you are and what a page covers, and Google recommends making sure it matches the visible text. Organization, LocalBusiness, Product, Article and FAQPage markup are common starting points. My schema markup service covers this in detail.

6. Strengthen your presence beyond your site

  • Keep Google Business Profile and Merchant Center details accurate. Google lists both in its AI features guidance.
  • Make sure your name, address, services and descriptions are consistent across directories and social profiles.
  • Earn mentions on reputable industry sites, local news and relevant community discussions. AI tools learn about brands from what others say, too.

7. Keep content fresh

  • Review your most important pages on a schedule and update facts, prices, screenshots and dates.
  • Remove or redirect outdated pages that could be quoted with old information.

How to measure your GEO strategy

Measurement is still the weakest part of GEO, so set expectations accordingly. Google Search Console counts traffic from AI features in the Performance report under the "Web" search type, together with regular results, so you can't separate it there. A few practical approaches:

  • Prompt tracking. Keep a list of the questions your customers ask, run them in Google, ChatGPT and other tools on a regular schedule, and record whether you're mentioned or cited.
  • Referral traffic in GA4. Visits from AI tools often show up with referrers such as chatgpt.com or perplexity.ai. Group them in a custom channel or exploration.
  • Branded search and direct traffic. People who see your name in an AI answer often search for you later rather than clicking straight through.
  • Leads. Ask new inquiries how they found you, and include AI tools as an option.

Common GEO mistakes to avoid

  • Chasing tricks. Keyword-stuffed "AI-friendly" pages and hidden text for bots can hurt you in regular search, which AI features depend on.
  • Blocking the wrong crawler. Blocking a search crawler because you meant to block a training crawler can quietly remove you from AI answers.
  • Neglecting the basics. Slow, thin or poorly linked pages rarely get cited, however well they're phrased.
  • Expecting guarantees. No one can promise a citation. Google itself notes that indexing and serving aren't guaranteed.

Is generative engine optimization replacing SEO?

No. GEO depends on SEO. Google's AI features draw on pages that are indexed and eligible for regular search results, and other AI tools rely on crawling and search indexes too. If your pages can't be crawled, rank poorly or say very little, they're unlikely to be cited. Think of GEO as SEO with extra attention on clear answers, quotable passages and your reputation across the web.

Do I need an llms.txt file or special markup for AI search?

Not for Google. Its AI features guidance says you don't need new machine-readable files, AI text files or special schema.org markup to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode. An llms.txt file is a proposed convention some sites use, but adding one is optional. Your time is usually better spent on crawl access, clear content and accurate structured data that matches the page.

How long does generative engine optimization take to work?

There's no fixed timeline. Changes like unblocking a crawler or fixing indexing issues can take effect as soon as pages are recrawled. Content and reputation work usually takes longer, because it depends on search engines reprocessing pages and on other sites mentioning you. Track a consistent set of prompts monthly so you can see whether citations and mentions are trending in the right direction.

Can small and local businesses benefit from GEO?

Yes, often more than large brands expect. People ask AI tools for local recommendations, comparisons and how-to answers. A complete Google Business Profile, consistent directory listings, genuine reviews and service pages that answer real customer questions all give AI tools clear information to work with. Local businesses with a focused niche can be easier to describe accurately than broad national brands.
